question: Under TRELA Section 1101.558(b-1), the written notice a license holder must provide at the time of first substantive communication regarding a specific property must, among other content, include:
choice_a: The license holder's name, license number, and contact information, printed in a minimum 10-point font
choice_b: The license holder's college transcript and continuing education certificates
choice_c: A complete copy of the multiple listing service data sheet for every property discussed
choice_d: The license holder's personal home address, regardless of business address
explanation: Section 1101.558(b-1) requires the written notice -- which describes how a broker can represent a party (including as an intermediary) and the license holder's basic duties -- to be printed in a minimum 10-point font and to identify the license holder by name, license number, and contact information, along with the sponsoring broker's information.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.558(b-1) (Representation Disclosure -- notice content and font-size requirement)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.558(c), the written notice describing representation and broker duties is NOT required when:
choice_a: The transaction involves a residential lease for not more than one year, and no sale of the property is being negotiated
choice_b: The transaction involves a commercial lease of any duration
choice_c: The buyer is purchasing a home for the first time
choice_d: The transaction value exceeds a statutory dollar threshold
explanation: Section 1101.558(c) exempts several specific situations from the written notice requirement, including a residential lease of not more than one year where no sale of the property is being negotiated -- since the low-stakes, short-term nature of such a lease does not implicate the same representation concerns as a sale.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.558(c) (Representation Disclosure -- exceptions, residential lease)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.558(c), a license holder who speaks with an unrepresented visitor at an open house about the property being shown is:
choice_a: Not required to provide the written representation-disclosure notice for that open house communication regarding that property
choice_b: Required to provide the written notice before the visitor may even enter the property
choice_c: Required to have the visitor sign a buyer representation agreement before speaking further
choice_d: In violation of TRELA merely by speaking with the visitor about the property
explanation: Section 1101.558(c) specifically exempts communications occurring at an open house regarding that property from the written notice requirement, recognizing the informal nature of open-house conversations with visitors who have not yet engaged the license holder in a transaction.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.558(c) (Representation Disclosure -- exceptions, open house)

question: Which of the following is one of the statutory exceptions under TRELA Section 1101.558(c) where the written representation-disclosure notice is not required?
choice_a: The other party is already known by the license holder to be represented by another license holder
choice_b: The property is being purchased entirely with cash rather than financing
choice_c: The seller has never sold real estate before
choice_d: The license holder has held an active license for more than ten years
explanation: Among the exceptions listed in Section 1101.558(c), written notice is not required when the license holder already knows the other party is represented by another license holder, since the core purpose of the notice -- informing an otherwise-uninformed party about representation -- is already satisfied in that situation.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.558(c) (Representation Disclosure -- exceptions, party already represented)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.559(a), the written consent required for a broker to act as an intermediary must, in addition to consenting to intermediary status, also:
choice_a: State the source of any expected compensation to the broker
choice_b: Waive the broker's obligation to act fairly and impartially
choice_c: Specify the exact anticipated closing date of the transaction
choice_d: Be independently notarized by a licensed notary public
explanation: Section 1101.559(a) requires that the written consent authorizing intermediary status also state the source of any compensation the broker expects to receive, ensuring the parties understand not just that the broker will act as intermediary but also how the broker is being paid.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559(a)(2) (Broker Acting as Intermediary -- consent must state source of compensation)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.559(b), a written listing agreement or buyer/tenant representation agreement can itself satisfy the intermediary written-consent requirement if it:
choice_a: Includes the consent language in prominent bold or underlined print identifying the conduct prohibited of an intermediary under Section 1101.651(d)
choice_b: Is signed by the sponsoring broker alone, without any signature from the party
choice_c: Is filed with TREC within 24 hours after signing
choice_d: Makes no reference whatsoever to intermediary status
explanation: Section 1101.559(b) allows the intermediary consent to be built into the listing agreement or buyer/tenant representation agreement itself, but only if that agreement includes the required language in prominent bold or underlined text identifying the conduct prohibited of an intermediary under Section 1101.651(d), so parties cannot overlook it.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559(b) (Broker Acting as Intermediary -- consent within listing/representation agreement)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.560(b), before an intermediary broker's appointment of associated license holders to work with each party takes effect, the broker must:
choice_a: Provide written notice of the appointment to all parties to the transaction
choice_b: Obtain TREC's advance individual approval of the specific appointees
choice_c: Wait until after closing to notify anyone of the appointment
choice_d: Appoint only license holders who have at least ten years of licensed experience
explanation: Section 1101.560(b) requires that, beyond the parties' written consent authorizing appointments in the first place, the broker also give written notice of the actual appointment to all transaction parties -- a separate procedural step from the underlying consent to appoint.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.560(b) (Associated License Holder Acting as Intermediary -- written notice of appointment)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.560, an associated license holder appointed to work with one specific party in an intermediary transaction is authorized to:
choice_a: Communicate with and execute instructions from that party, in addition to offering opinions and advice during negotiations
choice_b: Only relay messages verbatim, with no authority to execute any of the party's instructions
choice_c: Execute instructions from either party interchangeably, without being tied to a fixed appointment
choice_d: Represent both appointed parties simultaneously once appointed to either one
explanation: Section 1101.560 authorizes each appointed associated license holder to communicate with and execute instructions from the specific party to whom they are appointed, not merely to pass along messages -- while each appointment remains fixed to one party, not interchangeable between both sides.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.560(a),(c) (Associated License Holder Acting as Intermediary -- scope of appointed authority)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.651(d), an intermediary broker who discloses to a buyer that the seller will accept a price less than the asking price, without the seller's separate written authorization, has:
choice_a: Violated the statutory prohibition on disclosing a seller's willingness to accept a lower price
choice_b: Done nothing wrong, since an asking price is always public information
choice_c: Violated a duty owed only to the buyer, not the seller
choice_d: Complied with the broker's duty of full disclosure to the buyer
explanation: Section 1101.651(d) prohibits an intermediary from revealing that a seller or landlord will accept a price less than the asking price unless the seller has given separate written authorization -- the statutory counterpart to the prohibition on revealing a buyer's willingness to pay more than their offer.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651(d)(1) (Certain Practices Prohibited -- disclosure of seller's acceptable price)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.651(d), the general prohibition on an intermediary disclosing a party's confidential information does NOT apply when the information:
choice_a: Materially relates to the condition of the property
choice_b: Would help the broker close the transaction faster
choice_c: Was learned from a source outside the transaction
explanation: Section 1101.651(d) carves out an exception allowing disclosure of otherwise-confidential information when it materially relates to the condition of the property, since that category of information implicates separate disclosure duties (such as known defects) that the confidentiality rule is not meant to override.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651(d)(3) (Certain Practices Prohibited -- exception for property-condition information)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.651(d), an intermediary broker may disclose information a party specifically instructed be kept confidential if:
choice_a: Disclosure is required by law, such as under a court order
choice_b: The broker personally believes disclosure would speed up the transaction
choice_c: The other party simply asks for the information
choice_d: More than one offer has been received on the property
explanation: Section 1101.651(d) permits disclosure of a party's confidential information despite the general prohibition when disclosure is separately authorized in writing by the party, legally required (such as by court order), or materially relates to the property's condition -- but not merely because the broker or the other party finds disclosure convenient.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651(d)(3) (Certain Practices Prohibited -- exception for legally required disclosure)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.651(d), an intermediary's confidentiality obligation extends beyond the two statutorily named price disclosures to also cover:
choice_a: Any confidential information a party has specifically instructed the broker or sales agent, in writing, not to disclose
choice_b: Only information that is already a matter of public record
choice_c: Nothing beyond the two price-related disclosures named in the statute
choice_d: Only information relating to the buyer, never information relating to the seller
explanation: Beyond barring disclosure of a seller's acceptable-price floor or a buyer's offer ceiling, Section 1101.651(d) also broadly prohibits disclosing any confidential information, or information a party has specifically instructed in writing not to disclose, absent an applicable exception.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651(d)(3) (Certain Practices Prohibited -- scope of confidentiality beyond price)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.561, the statutory duties of a license holder acting as an intermediary:
choice_a: Supersede the duties otherwise established for a license holder under any other law, including common law
choice_b: Apply only after common-law fiduciary duties have first been fully satisfied
choice_c: Are void whenever they conflict with common-law agency principles
choice_d: Apply only to transactions valued above a statutory dollar threshold
explanation: Section 1101.561 provides that the duties of a license holder acting as an intermediary supersede the duties otherwise established under any other law, including common law -- meaning traditional common-law agency duties (such as undivided loyalty to a single principal) do not override the statutory intermediary framework.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.561(a) (Duties of Intermediary Prevail)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.561(b), if a broker agrees to represent both a buyer or tenant and a seller or landlord in the same transaction, the broker:
choice_a: Must agree to act as an intermediary in that transaction
choice_b: May instead choose to represent only whichever party pays a commission
choice_c: Is barred from representing either party any further once both have signed
choice_d: May represent both without any special status, since intermediary status is always optional
explanation: Section 1101.561(b) makes intermediary status mandatory, not optional, once a broker agrees to represent both a buyer/tenant and a seller/landlord in the same transaction -- a broker cannot represent both sides of a deal while declining the intermediary framework designed to manage that dual representation.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.561(b) (Duties of Intermediary Prevail -- mandatory intermediary status)
